title: Poets at the fair
hook: at the fairs of 'Ukaz poets competed, and the best odes were honored

segments.voice: Yesterday, qabilah, the tribe. Your line was: belonging protected you.

Dust, tents, the smell of leather and spice. Traders have come from across the peninsula to a market called 'Ukaz. But one crowd isn't gathered around the goods. It's gathered around a man standing up to speak. A long poem comes out, measured and rhymed, line after line landing on the same sound. When he finishes, people repeat his best lines to each other. By the time the caravans leave, those lines will travel farther than any bale of cloth. Today: poets at the fair.
screen: `A MARKET CALLED 'UKAZ.` → `A CROWD AROUND A SPEAKER.` → `LINES THAT TRAVEL.`

segments.voice: Ibn Abbas, a young cousin of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, names 'Ukaz in Sahih al-Bukhari as one of the markets of the days before Islam. Later writers remember it as a place where poets performed and were judged. The Arabic word for poet is sha'ir. Poems that come down from that time praised a tribe's courage, mourned the dead, described a camel, or lingered over an abandoned campsite where a beloved once lived. Tradition says a great poem could make a tribe famous, and a mocking one could shame it. Later writers gathered a set of odes called the Mu'allaqat, the hung ones, and a story people tell says they were hung on the Ka'ba. That story is disputed, and the name's first meaning is uncertain. So when the Qur'an came, it came to listeners who knew good language the way some people know good bread. Some in Mecca called the Prophet a poet; surah fifty-two quotes them saying so. The Qur'an answers directly. Surah thirty-six says Allah did not teach him poetry, and that it does not befit him. Surah sixty-nine says this is not the speech of a poet. That isn't the Qur'an calling poetry worthless. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says that some poetry is wisdom. It is the Qur'an saying: this is something else. And the people best placed to hear the difference were the ones who had stood in the crowd at 'Ukaz, and knew exactly what a poem sounded like.
screen: `'UKAZ: A MARKET BEFORE ISLAM.` · `SHA'IR: POET.` · `THE HUNG ODES, AND A DISPUTED STORY.` · `NOT THE SPEECH OF A POET.` · then, large: `SOME POETRY IS WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Find one line you love, a verse a grandparent used to quote, a lyric, a few words of the Qur'an if you know them, and say it aloud slowly, then once more, softer, listening for where it rises and which word carries the weight. Then sit in the quiet after it. If you pray, you can thank Allah for the gift of speech; if you don't, simply notice what a few words just did to the room.
Sha'ir. Poet: at 'Ukaz and markets like it, these men recited and were judged, and a good line could travel farther than any caravan. Today's word.
Your line: words had power. Tomorrow, the House among the idols. Seven hundred days now.

screen: `DAY 700 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HOUSE AMONG THE IDOLS.`

howItsDone: Classical Arabic poetry from before Islam is still studied by Muslims and students of Arabic, partly to understand the language the Qur'an's first listeners knew; the Qur'an itself is recited, not sung as poetry.

what it means: a market where poems carried a tribe's honor, and crowds knew good language when they heard it.
what a scholar hears: the Qur'an's first listeners knew poetry well; when it says it is not a poet's speech (36:69, 69:41), it is speaking to that crowd.

notes: Bukhari numbers cited from memory: Ibn Abbas on 'Ukaz, Majanna and Dhu'l-Majaz (2050; also 1770 and 4519 in the tafsir of 2:198) and 'some poetry is wisdom' (6145); confirm.
Sha'ir glossed from a root linked to knowing and perceiving (sh-'-r); confirm against a standard lexicon.
The Mu'allaqat are named without a count; the hanging-on-the-Ka'ba story is framed as told and disputed; confirm.
'Later writers remember it as a place where poets performed and were judged': the judging details are from later adab literature, not Bukhari; confirm wording.
